description: Combined test: Chemistry + Physics for JEE MAINS. 40Q.

instructions: Section A: MCQ questions — all compulsory (+4/-1)
Section B: Numerical value questions — no negative marking
Correct MCQ: +4 marks | Wrong MCQ: -1 mark
Numerical: +4 marks correct | 0 marks wrong (no penalty)
Enter numerical answers as integers rounded to nearest value

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for an aromatic compound to undergo nucleophilic aromatic substitution via the benzyne mechanism?

options.text: Presence of a strong electron-withdrawing group ortho/para to the halogen
options.explanation: This is required for addition-elimination NAS, not benzyne.

options.text: Strong base (e.g., NaNH₂) to abstract a proton
options.explanation: Strong base is required to form the benzyne intermediate.

options.text: Highly activated ring (e.g., nitro groups) for addition-elimination pathway
options.explanation: This describes the addition-elimination NAS, not the benzyne mechanism.

options.text: Halogen atom directly attached to the aromatic ring
options.explanation: A halogen is required for both mechanisms.

questions.explanation: The benzyne mechanism does not require strong electron-withdrawing groups (unlike the addition-elimination NAS). It occurs in unsubstituted aryl halides (e.g., chlorobenzene) with strong bases. Option C describes the standard NAS mechanism (e.g., with –NO₂ groups), not benzyne.
questions.hint: Benzyne mechanism occurs in unsubstituted or weakly activated aryl halides under strong base and high temperature.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Predict the major product when 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene is treated with NaOH at high temperature.

options.explanation: The nitro group activates the ring for addition-elimination NAS, replacing Cl with OH.
This would require replacement of OH with Cl, which does not occur.
This would require replacement of Cl with NO₂, which does not occur.
The reaction proceeds via addition-elimination NAS.

questions.explanation: The nitro group (–NO₂) is a strong electron-withdrawing group that activates the ring for addition-elimination NAS. OH⁻ replaces Cl at the position ortho/para to –NO₂, yielding 1-hydroxy-4-nitrobenzene.
questions.hint: The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing group that directs nucleophilic substitution.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following aryl halides will undergo nucleophilic aromatic substitution (NAS) the fastest with NaOCH₃ in methanol?

options.explanation: No electron-withdrawing groups present, so NAS is slow.
Two strong electron-withdrawing groups (nitro) make this the most activated for NAS.
Only one electron-withdrawing group present, and it is meta, so less activation.
One strong electron-withdrawing group present, but less activated than 1-Chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene.

questions.explanation: NAS rate depends on electron-withdrawing groups (EWGs) and their positions. The ortho/para effect makes 2,4-dinitro the most activated (two strong EWGs), leading to the fastest substitution. Other options have fewer or less activating EWGs.
questions.hint: The presence of multiple strong electron-withdrawing groups ortho/para to the halogen increases the rate of NAS.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: In the reaction of 1-fluoro-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene with CH₃ONa, the leaving group ability follows the order:

options.explanation: F⁻ is the best leaving group in NAS due to its high electronegativity and small size.
This is the order for SN2/SN1 reactions, not NAS.
This order does not align with the stability of the leaving anion in NAS.
This order does not reflect the stability of the leaving anion in NAS.

questions.explanation: In NAS, the leaving group ability is influenced by the strength of the C–X bond and the stability of the leaving anion. F⁻ is the best leaving group due to its high electronegativity and small size, despite having the strongest C–F bond. This order (F > Cl > Br > I) is unique to NAS and differs from SN2/SN1.
questions.hint: In NAS, the stability of the leaving anion (F⁻) and electronegativity play a key role in determining the leaving group ability.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following conditions would favor the benzyne mechanism over the addition-elimination mechanism in aryl halides?

options.text: Presence of a strong electron-withdrawing group (e.g., –NO₂)
options.explanation: This favors the addition-elimination mechanism, not benzyne.

options.text: Use of a mild nucleophile (e.g., H₂O)
options.explanation: Mild nucleophiles do not favor benzyne formation; strong bases are required.

options.text: Absence of strongly activating groups and high temperature
options.explanation: These conditions favor the benzyne mechanism in aryl halides.
Polar aprotic solvents are not specific to benzyne formation.

questions.explanation: The benzyne mechanism occurs in unsubstituted or weakly activated aryl halides under strong base and high temperature, where no EWGs are present to stabilize the Meisenheimer complex.
questions.hint: Benzyne mechanism requires the absence of strongly activating groups and high temperature for strong base activation.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: A student treats 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene with NaOH at 100°C. The student expects the product to be 3-bromophenol. However, the major product is 3-nitrophenol. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The reaction proceeds via the benzyne mechanism, and the nucleophile attacks the benzyne intermediate at the meta position.
options.explanation: The benzyne mechanism explains the formation of 3-nitrophenol from 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene.

options.text: The nitro group migrates under the reaction conditions.
options.explanation: Nitro groups do not migrate under these conditions.

options.text: The bromine is replaced by OH⁻ via addition-elimination.
options.explanation: Addition-elimination would place OH ortho/para to the nitro group, not meta.

options.text: The reaction is reversible, and thermodynamic control favors 3-nitrophenol.
options.explanation: Thermodynamic control does not explain this outcome.

questions.explanation: In meta-nitro aryl halides, the benzyne mechanism dominates because the nitro group is not ortho/para to the halogen, preventing effective stabilization of the Meisenheimer complex. The nucleophile (OH⁻) attacks the benzyne intermediate, leading to substitution at the meta position relative to the nitro group.
questions.hint: When the electron-withdrawing group is meta to the halogen, the benzyne mechanism is favored over addition-elimination.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following statements about nucleophilic aromatic substitution (NAS) is INCORRECT?

options.text: The addition-elimination mechanism requires electron-withdrawing groups ortho/para to the halogen.
options.explanation: This is a correct statement about addition-elimination NAS.

options.text: The benzyne mechanism can occur in aryl halides without activating groups.
options.explanation: This is a correct statement about the benzyne mechanism.

options.text: Fluoride is a better leaving group than iodide in NAS due to the strong C–F bond.
options.explanation: This statement is incorrect because the strong C–F bond does not make F⁻ a better leaving group; its high electronegativity and small size do.

options.text: NAS is favored by polar aprotic solvents like DMSO.
options.explanation: This is a correct statement about NAS.

questions.explanation: While F⁻ is the best leaving group in NAS due to its high electronegativity and small size (despite the strong C–F bond), the reason given in C is misleading. The statement incorrectly attributes the reason to the bond strength rather than the stability of F⁻.
questions.hint: The leaving group ability in NAS is primarily due to the stability of the leaving anion, not the bond strength.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: An aryl halide X undergoes NAS with NaOH to give a product where the OH group is meta to a nitro group. Which of the following could be X?

options.explanation: This would yield a product with OH ortho/para to the nitro group via addition-elimination.
This undergoes benzyne mechanism, placing OH meta to the nitro group.
This would yield a product with OH ortho/para to the nitro groups via addition-elimination.
This would yield a product with OH ortho to the nitro group via addition-elimination.

questions.explanation: For the OH group to be meta to the nitro group, the reaction must proceed via the benzyne mechanism. 1-Chloro-3-nitrobenzene has no ortho/para EWGs to stabilize the Meisenheimer complex, forcing benzyne formation. The nucleophile attacks the benzyne intermediate at the meta position relative to the nitro group.
questions.hint: A meta-nitro aryl halide without ortho/para electron-withdrawing groups will undergo benzyne mechanism, placing the OH group meta to the nitro group.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: In the reaction of 1-iodo-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene with CH₃OH, the rate-determining step is:

options.explanation: The formation of the Meisenheimer complex is the rate-determining step in highly activated aryl halides.

options.text: Loss of I⁻ from the Meisenheimer complex
options.explanation: This is a fast step after the Meisenheimer complex is formed.
This is also a fast step after the Meisenheimer complex is formed.
This is the same as the formation of the Meisenheimer complex, which is the rate-determining step.

questions.explanation: In strongly activated aryl halides (e.g., 2,4,6-trinitro), the rate-determining step is the formation of the Meisenheimer complex (addition of the nucleophile to the ring), not the leaving group departure or deprotonation.
questions.hint: In highly activated aryl halides, the slow step is the formation of the Meisenheimer complex due to the electron-deficient nature of the ring.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: What is the most common mechanism for nucleophilic aromatic substitution in aryl halides under normal conditions?

options.explanation: Electrophilic addition-elimination is not a common mechanism for nucleophilic aromatic substitution.
The benzyne mechanism is the most common under normal conditions for unactivated aryl halides.
Free radical substitution is not a typical mechanism for aryl halides.
SN2 displacement is not feasible for aryl halides due to the sp2 hybridized carbon.

questions.explanation: Aryl halides typically do not undergo SN2 or electrophilic substitution directly. The benzyne mechanism (elimination-addition) is emphasized for unactivated aryl halides under normal conditions, especially in the JEE context.
questions.hint: Consider the reactivity of aryl halides with strong bases.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following aryl halides is most reactive toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution via the benzyne mechanism?

options.explanation: Chlorobenzene is less reactive compared to fluorobenzene in the benzyne mechanism.
Bromobenzene is less reactive compared to fluorobenzene in the benzyne mechanism.
Fluorobenzene is the most reactive due to the high electronegativity of fluorine.
Iodobenzene is less reactive compared to fluorobenzene in the benzyne mechanism.

questions.explanation: Fluorobenzene is the most reactive due to the high electronegativity of fluorine, which facilitates the elimination step in the benzyne mechanism.
questions.hint: Consider the strength of the carbon-halogen bond and the leaving group ability.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: In nucleophilic aromatic substitution, which factor does NOT favor the addition-elimination mechanism?

options.text: Presence of electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., –NO2) ortho or para to the halogen
options.explanation: Electron-withdrawing groups favor the addition-elimination mechanism by stabilizing the intermediate.

options.text: Use of a non-polar solvent like hexane
options.explanation: Non-polar solvents do not stabilize the anionic intermediate formed during addition.

options.text: Use of a strong nucleophile such as OH−
options.explanation: Strong nucleophiles favor the addition-elimination mechanism.
High temperatures favor the addition-elimination mechanism.

questions.explanation: The addition-elimination mechanism is favored by polar aprotic solvents or high temperatures, not non-polar solvents like hexane.
questions.hint: Consider the stabilization of intermediates in different solvents.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Which compound is expected to undergo nucleophilic aromatic substitution most readily under mild conditions?

options.explanation: Chlorobenzene is less reactive without activating groups.
p-Chlorotoluene is less activated compared to 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene.
The nitro groups strongly activate the ring for nucleophilic substitution.
Benzyl chloride undergoes substitution via SN2 or SN1, not nucleophilic aromatic substitution.

questions.explanation: 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene has three electron-withdrawing nitro groups that strongly activate the ring toward nucleophilic substitution via the addition-elimination mechanism.
questions.hint: Consider the effect of electron-withdrawing groups on aryl halides.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: What is the major product when chlorobenzene is treated with NaNH2 in liquid ammonia?

options.explanation: Aniline is formed after the benzyne intermediate is attacked by NH2−, but the major product is derived from the benzyne intermediate.

options.text: Benzyne intermediate followed by formation of aniline
options.explanation: The benzyne intermediate is formed first, leading to aniline as the major product.
Phenol is not the major product in this reaction.
Benzylamine is not formed in this reaction.

questions.explanation: Chlorobenzene undergoes elimination to form benzyne when treated with NaNH2, which is then attacked by NH2− to form aniline.
questions.hint: Consider the benzyne mechanism and the role of NaNH2.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the reactivity of aryl halides toward nucleophilic substitution?

options.text: Aryl halides undergo SN2 reactions more readily than alkyl halides due to resonance stabilization
options.explanation: Aryl halides do not undergo SN2 reactions readily due to the sp2 hybridized carbon.

options.text: Aryl halides react with nucleophiles via direct SN1 mechanism
options.explanation: Aryl halides do not typically undergo SN1 reactions.

options.text: Aryl halides with electron-withdrawing groups ortho/para to the halogen are activated for nucleophilic substitution
options.explanation: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the intermediate, increasing reactivity.

options.text: Aryl halides do not react with nucleophiles under any conditions
options.explanation: Aryl halides can react with nucleophiles under specific conditions.

questions.explanation: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the Meisenheimer complex formed during nucleophilic aromatic substitution, making the aryl halide more reactive.
questions.hint: Consider the role of substituents on the aromatic ring.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: In a reaction involving nucleophilic aromatic substitution, if the substituent is –OCH3 at the para position to the halogen, the rate of substitution is:

options.explanation: The –OCH3 group deactivates the ring, making substitution slower.
The electron-donating group deactivates the ring, reducing the rate of substitution.
The rate is affected by the presence of the –OCH3 group.
The primary factor here is the electronic effect of the substituent.

questions.explanation: The –OCH3 group is electron-donating and deactivates the ring toward nucleophilic substitution by stabilizing the ring and making the addition step less favorable.
questions.hint: Consider the electronic effect of the methoxy group.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following solvents is most suitable for nucleophilic aromatic substitution via the addition-elimination mechanism?

options.explanation: Hexane is a non-polar solvent and does not stabilize the intermediates.
Diethyl ether is a polar aprotic solvent but less effective than DMSO for this mechanism.
DMSO is a polar aprotic solvent that stabilizes the intermediates well.
Benzene is a non-polar solvent and does not favor the addition-elimination mechanism.

questions.explanation: Polar aprotic solvents like DMSO stabilize cations and anions without hydrogen bonding, which is ideal for the addition-elimination mechanism.
questions.hint: Consider the properties of solvents that favor the addition-elimination mechanism.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: A student performs a reaction with p-nitrochlorobenzene and NaOH at room temperature. What is the most likely product?

options.explanation: p-Nitrobenzyl alcohol is not formed in this reaction.
The chlorine is replaced by –OH to form p-nitrophenol.
p-Nitroaniline is not formed in this reaction.
Chlorobenzene is the starting material, not the product.

questions.explanation: p-Nitrochlorobenzene undergoes nucleophilic aromatic substitution via the addition-elimination mechanism due to the strong electron-withdrawing nitro group. The chlorine is replaced by –OH to form p-nitrophenol.
questions.hint: Consider the activating effect of the nitro group on the aryl halide.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: In the benzyne mechanism, what is the intermediate formed when chlorobenzene reacts with NaNH2?

options.explanation: Benzyne is the intermediate formed in the benzyne mechanism.
Phenyl anion is not formed in the benzyne mechanism.
Chlorobenzene radical is not an intermediate in the benzyne mechanism.
Cyclohexadienyl anion is not formed in the benzyne mechanism.

questions.explanation: The benzyne mechanism involves the elimination of HCl from chlorobenzene to form benzyne (dehydrobenzene), a highly reactive intermediate with a triple bond in the benzene ring.
questions.hint: Consider the elimination step in the benzyne mechanism.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: Consider the following reaction sequence involving an aryl halide: CH₃–C₆H₄–Br + NaOH (aq, 200°C) → ? Which one of the following statements correctly describes the major organic product formed under these conditions?

options.text: The product is CH₃–C₆H₄–OH via a direct SN2 displacement on the aryl carbon.
options.explanation: SN2 displacement on an aryl carbon is highly unfavorable due to the sp2 hybridization and steric hindrance. Aryl halides do not undergo SN2 reactions.

options.text: The product is CH₃–C₆H₄–OH formed via an elimination-addition (benzyne) mechanism.
options.explanation: While the benzyne mechanism is correct, this option does not account for the fact that benzyne formation is not dependent on the presence of electron-withdrawing groups under these conditions.

options.text: The product is CH₃–C₆H₄–OH formed via a concerted addition-elimination (SNAr) mechanism.
options.explanation: SNAr (addition-elimination) requires the aromatic ring to be activated by strong electron-withdrawing groups. This is not the case here.

options.text: The product is CH₃–C₆H₄–OH formed via an elimination-addition (benzyne) mechanism only if the aromatic ring is activated by strong electron-withdrawing groups.
options.explanation: This option incorrectly states that benzyne formation requires activation by electron-withdrawing groups. Under high-temperature aqueous NaOH conditions, benzyne formation occurs even without activation.

questions.explanation: Aryl halides typically do not undergo direct SN2 or SNAr (addition-elimination) mechanisms unless the aromatic ring is strongly activated by electron-withdrawing groups like –NO₂ or –CN. Under the given conditions (high temperature and aqueous NaOH), the benzyne (elimination-addition) mechanism is the most feasible pathway, leading to the formation of phenol (CH₃–C₆H₄–OH). Option D correctly states that benzyne formation occurs even without activation under these forcing conditions.
questions.hint: Recall the mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution in aryl halides. SN2 and SNAr require specific conditions, while benzyne formation is favored under high-temperature aqueous NaOH conditions.
questions.subject: jee-chemistry

questions.question: The Davisson-Germer experiment is primarily used to demonstrate which fundamental property of matter?

options.explanation: The photoelectric effect demonstrates the particle nature of light, not necessarily matter.
The Compton effect shows the particle nature of light (photons) interacting with matter.
The experiment confirmed the wave nature of electrons by observing diffraction patterns.
The particle nature of light was demonstrated by the Compton effect and photoelectric effect, not Davisson-Germer.

questions.explanation: The Davisson-Germer experiment observed diffraction patterns when electrons were scattered off a nickel crystal, which directly demonstrated the wave nature of electrons (de Broglie wavelength). This was a key confirmation of quantum mechanics.
questions.hint: Think about what kind of patterns are formed when waves interact with a periodic structure.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer setup, if the accelerating voltage for electrons is increased from 54 V to 216 V, how does the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons change?

options.explanation: The wavelength changes with voltage, as per the de Broglie formula.
Doubling would occur if voltage decreased, not increased.
Increasing voltage by 4 times reduces the wavelength by half.
Quadrupling would imply a much smaller change in voltage or an inverse relationship.

questions.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength λ = h/√(2meV). If V becomes 4 times (216/54), λ becomes 1/√4 = 1/2 times the original wavelength. Thus, the wavelength halves.
questions.hint: Recall the relationship between accelerating voltage and electron wavelength.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: Which of the following observations in the Davisson-Germer experiment confirmed the wave nature of matter?

options.text: Emission of electrons from a metal surface
options.explanation: Emission of electrons is related to the photoelectric effect, not wave nature.
Diffraction patterns are a definitive proof of wave nature.
A continuous spectrum is not uniquely indicative of wave nature.

options.text: Reflection of electrons at specific angles
options.explanation: Reflection can occur for both waves and particles, so it is not definitive.

questions.explanation: The observation of a diffraction pattern (similar to X-ray diffraction) confirmed that electrons exhibit wave-like behavior, as diffraction is a wave phenomenon.
questions.hint: Diffraction is a characteristic behavior of waves.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: If the spacing between atomic planes in the nickel crystal used in Davisson-Germer experiment is 0.091 nm and the first-order diffraction maximum occurs at 65°, what is the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons?

options.explanation: This value does not match the calculation using Bragg's law.
This matches the calculated wavelength using the given parameters.
This value is slightly higher than the calculated result.
This value is significantly higher than the calculated result.

questions.hint: Use Bragg's law: nλ = 2d sinθ.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: Which of the following statements best explains why the Davisson-Germer experiment used a nickel crystal instead of a regular metal surface?

options.text: Nickel has a high work function
options.explanation: Work function is unrelated to the ability to produce diffraction patterns.

options.text: Nickel atoms are arranged in a crystalline structure that acts as a 3D diffraction grating
options.explanation: The crystalline structure provides the necessary periodic potential for diffraction.

options.text: Nickel emits more electrons under electron bombardment
options.explanation: Electron emission is not the primary reason for using a crystal.

options.text: Nickel has a low melting point
options.explanation: Melting point is irrelevant to the experiment's purpose.

questions.explanation: The crystalline structure of nickel acts as a 3D diffraction grating, allowing electron waves to interfere constructively and produce diffraction patterns, similar to X-rays in Bragg's law.
questions.hint: Consider the structural properties required for diffraction to occur.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, if the angle of scattering is increased from 40° to 80°, how does the intensity of the diffracted electron beam change?

options.explanation: The intensity does not increase continuously with angle.
The intensity does not decrease continuously with angle.

options.text: It first increases and then decreases
options.explanation: The intensity shows peaks and troughs due to interference effects.
The intensity varies with angle due to interference.

questions.explanation: The intensity of the diffracted beam depends on the constructive and destructive interference of electron waves. At certain angles (like 50°), the intensity peaks due to constructive interference, while at other angles, it decreases due to destructive interference.
questions.hint: Consider how interference patterns vary with angle.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: The Davisson-Germer experiment was initially designed to study:

options.explanation: The photoelectric effect was studied by Einstein, not Davisson-Germer.

options.text: The scattering of electrons by a metal surface
options.explanation: The experiment was designed to study electron scattering.

options.text: The emission of X-rays from metals
options.explanation: X-ray emission was studied by other experiments, like those by Roentgen.
Ionization of gases was studied by other experiments, not Davisson-Germer.

questions.explanation: The experiment was originally intended to study the reflection of electrons from a metal surface, but the observation of diffraction patterns was an unexpected discovery that confirmed the wave nature of electrons.
questions.hint: Consider the original intent of the experiment before the discovery.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: If the de Broglie wavelength of electrons in the Davisson-Germer experiment is 0.165 nm, what is the minimum accelerating voltage required to produce this wavelength?

options.explanation: This value is slightly lower than the calculated result.
This matches the calculated accelerating voltage.
This value is higher than the calculated result.
This value is significantly higher than the calculated result.

questions.hint: Use the de Broglie wavelength formula and solve for accelerating voltage V.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the role of the nickel crystal in the Davisson-Germer experiment?

options.text: It acts as a source of electrons
options.explanation: The nickel crystal does not emit electrons; it scatters them.

options.text: It acts as a filter for specific wavelengths
options.explanation: A filter would selectively allow certain wavelengths, but the crystal acts as a diffraction grating.

options.text: It acts as a 3D diffraction grating for electron waves
options.explanation: The regular atomic spacing in the crystal causes diffraction of electron waves.
The crystal scatters electrons rather than absorbing them.

questions.explanation: The nickel crystal's atomic planes are spaced regularly, acting as a 3D diffraction grating that causes electron waves to interfere and produce diffraction patterns, analogous to X-ray diffraction.
questions.hint: Think about how a crystal structure can affect wave behavior.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: Suppose the Davisson-Germer experiment is repeated with electrons accelerated to a very high speed (relativistic regime). Which of the following modifications must be made to the de Broglie wavelength formula?

options.text: Use λ = h/p, where p = mv
options.explanation: This formula is non-relativistic and does not account for high speeds.
This formula is also non-relativistic and assumes low speeds.

options.text: Use λ = h/(γmv), where γ is the Lorentz factor
options.explanation: This formula accounts for relativistic effects on momentum.
This formula is used for photons, not electrons.

questions.explanation: At relativistic speeds, momentum p = γmv (where γ = 1/√(1 - v²/c²)), so the de Broglie wavelength must account for this relativistic momentum: λ = h/(γmv). Ignoring relativity would lead to incorrect results for high-speed electrons.
questions.hint: Consider how relativistic effects alter the momentum of high-speed particles.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: Which of the following observations in the Davisson-Germer experiment confirmed the wave nature of electrons?

options.text: The electrons were deflected by magnetic fields like charged particles
options.explanation: This observation is consistent with electron charge but does not confirm wave nature.

options.text: The intensity of scattered electrons showed a maximum at specific angles
options.explanation: Diffraction maxima are a hallmark of wave interference, confirming the wave nature of electrons.

options.text: The electrons produced a continuous spectrum on the detector screen
options.explanation: A continuous spectrum is not indicative of wave diffraction.

options.text: The electrons exhibited a constant stopping potential independent of voltage
options.explanation: Stopping potential relates to energy conservation, not wave nature.

questions.explanation: The Davisson-Germer experiment observed diffraction patterns (maxima at specific angles), which are characteristic of wave behavior. This confirmed electron wave nature via Bragg's law.
questions.hint: Consider the nature of the observed diffraction pattern.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, if the accelerating potential V is increased, how does the de Broglie wavelength λ of the electrons change?

options.explanation: The wavelength does not increase linearly with V.
The wavelength is inversely proportional to the square root of the accelerating potential.
The wavelength changes with the accelerating potential.
The wavelength does not increase with the square root of V.

questions.explanation: de Broglie wavelength for electrons accelerated by potential V is λ = h/√(2meV). Thus, λ ∝ 1/√V. Increasing V decreases λ.
questions.hint: Recall the relation between de Broglie wavelength and kinetic energy of electrons.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: The Davisson-Germer experiment used a nickel crystal with lattice spacing d = 0.091 nm. For an electron beam with de Broglie wavelength λ = 0.048 nm, the angle θ for first-order diffraction (n=1) satisfies Bragg’s law as:

options.explanation: This is the correct calculation using Bragg's law.
This value is double the correct calculation.
This option involves cosine, which is not relevant here.
This option involves tangent, which is not relevant here.

questions.explanation: Bragg's law: nλ = 2d sinθ. For n=1, sinθ = λ/(2d) = 0.048/(2×0.091) ≈ 0.264.
questions.hint: Use Bragg's law (nλ = 2d sinθ) to calculate the required angle.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct statement about the Davisson-Germer experiment setup?

options.text: A heated filament emits electrons which are accelerated toward a nickel crystal
options.explanation: This is a correct statement about the setup.

options.text: The scattered electrons are detected by a movable Faraday cup connected to a galvanometer
options.explanation: This is a correct description of the detection method.

options.text: The experiment was initially designed to study electron reflection, not diffraction
options.explanation: This is incorrect; the experiment was not initially designed for diffraction.

options.text: The observed diffraction pattern matched predictions from wave theory
options.explanation: This is a correct statement about the results.

questions.explanation: The Davisson-Germer experiment was originally aimed at studying electron reflection, but accidental oxidation of the nickel target led to the discovery of electron diffraction, confirming wave nature.
questions.hint: Consider the original intent versus the actual outcome of the experiment.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: If the accelerating voltage in the Davisson-Germer experiment is doubled, by what factor does the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons change?

options.explanation: The wavelength does not increase.
The wavelength decreases by a factor of √2 when the voltage is doubled.
The wavelength changes with the voltage.
The wavelength does not increase by a factor of 2.

questions.explanation: λ ∝ 1/√V. If V → 2V, λ → λ/√2. So the wavelength decreases by a factor of √2.
questions.hint: Use the relation between de Broglie wavelength and accelerating potential.
questions.subject: jee-physics

questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, the intensity of scattered electrons shows maxima at certain angles. These maxima can be explained by:

options.explanation: The photoelectric effect explains electron emission, not diffraction.
Bragg's law explains the diffraction maxima observed in the experiment.
Compton scattering involves photon-electron interactions, not diffraction.
The uncertainty principle does not explain diffraction patterns.

questions.question: Which experimental observation would most directly contradict the Davisson-Germer result if it were observed?

options.text: Electrons scattered in all directions with uniform intensity
options.explanation: This would indicate no diffraction, contradicting the wave nature of electrons.

options.text: A continuous spectrum of scattered electrons without peaks
options.explanation: A continuous spectrum without peaks would indicate no diffraction maxima.

options.text: Electrons producing a single bright spot on the detector
options.explanation: A single bright spot could still be consistent with wave interference depending on setup.

options.text: Electrons showing interference patterns in a double-slit setup
options.explanation: This would support the wave nature of electrons, not contradict it.

questions.explanation: Uniform intensity without peaks would contradict the wave diffraction pattern predicted by Bragg’s law and observed in the experiment.

questions.question: If the Davisson-Germer experiment were conducted using protons instead of electrons (same accelerating voltage), how would the diffraction angle θ change? (Assume proton mass mp ≈ 1836 me)

options.text: θ would increase because protons have a longer de Broglie wavelength
options.explanation: Protons have a shorter de Broglie wavelength due to their larger mass.

options.text: θ would decrease because protons have a shorter de Broglie wavelength
options.explanation: A shorter wavelength leads to a smaller diffraction angle.
The angle changes due to the different wavelengths.

options.text: θ would depend on the crystal lattice spacing only

questions.explanation: de Broglie wavelength λ = h/√(2mK.E.). Since mp >> me, λ for protons is much smaller than for electrons. Thus, sinθ = λ/(2d) decreases → θ decreases.

questions.question: Which of the following modifications to the Davisson-Germer experiment would make the diffraction pattern less pronounced?

options.explanation: Increasing voltage makes the pattern sharper.

options.text: Using a crystal with smaller lattice spacing
options.explanation: Smaller lattice spacing can make the pattern sharper.

options.text: Decreasing the number of atoms in the crystal (e.g., using a thin film instead of bulk)
options.explanation: Fewer atoms reduce constructive interference, weakening the pattern.

options.text: Increasing the temperature of the crystal
options.explanation: Temperature affects atomic vibrations but not the number of scattering centers.

questions.explanation: A thinner crystal (fewer atomic layers) reduces the number of scattering centers, weakening the constructive interference and making the diffraction pattern less sharp.
